client: I've been really struggling lately with keeping up my GPA while also working at the cafe a few nights a week. It feels like no matter how much I try, I'm always falling short somewhere — either my grades slip or I miss a shift, and then I just feel terrible about myself. I honestly don't know if talking about it is going to change anything, because the pressure is still going to be there whether I talk about it or not.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy load right now — trying to hold everything together while feeling like you're constantly coming up short, and that exhaustion comes through clearly in how you're describing it. I also notice there's a part of you that's skeptical about whether talking will even help, which makes a lot of sense when the pressure feels so relentless and real. I'm curious — when you say you feel terrible about yourself in those moments, what does that inner voice actually say to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: It usually says something like "you're a burden to everyone around you" or "people only put up with you, they don't actually want you there." And then it kind of spirals from there into this feeling that I'm fundamentally broken in some way that can't be fixed. It's embarrassing to even say out loud, honestly, because part of me knows it sounds dramatic, but in the moment it feels completely true.
therapist: Thank you for trusting me with that — it takes real courage to say those things out loud, and I want you to know it doesn't sound dramatic at all; it sounds like genuine pain. That voice that calls you a burden or "fundamentally broken" is incredibly common in people who are pushing themselves hard, and in CBT we'd call it a core belief — something that feels like absolute truth in the moment but is actually a story, not a fact. I'm wondering, when that spiral starts, is there ever a small part of you that pushes back on it, even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, sometimes there is this tiny part of me that thinks "wait, that's not completely true" — like a flicker before the louder voice just drowns it out. But it's so faint and it disappears so fast that it almost feels pointless to hold onto it. I guess I'm skeptical that noticing that small voice would actually change anything, because the spiral always wins in the end anyway.
therapist: That flicker you're describing — that quiet "wait, that's not completely true" — is actually really significant, even if it feels impossibly small right now, because it means some part of you hasn't fully bought into that harsh story about yourself. I notice as you talk about it, there's something that sounds almost tired underneath your words, like you want to believe that flicker matters but you've been disappointed before. What do you think would need to happen for that small voice to feel even just a little more worth listening to?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, you're right that I'm tired. I've had these little moments of doubt about the harsh things I tell myself before, and I've tried to hold onto them, but then something happens — like I reach out to someone and they don't respond, or I'm sitting alone on a Friday night again — and that small voice just gets completely drowned out. I guess what would need to happen is for the flicker to actually lead somewhere, like for it to matter in real life, not just in my head during a therapy session.
therapist: What you're describing makes so much sense — it's hard to hold onto that flicker when real moments, like reaching out and being met with silence, seem to confirm the louder voice all over again. Those moments of sitting alone or not getting a response aren't just neutral events; they become "evidence" that the harsh story is true, even when there might be other explanations. I'm curious about one of those specific moments — when someone didn't respond, what did you tell yourself was the reason why?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I told myself they probably just didn't want to deal with me, like I was too much or too boring to bother responding to. It's this immediate jump my brain makes — like silence equals rejection, and rejection equals proof that I'm just not worth the effort. And the worst part is, even when I try to think of other reasons, like maybe they were busy or distracted, it just doesn't stick the way that first thought does.
therapist: You've just described something really important — your brain has essentially built a fast, automatic highway straight from "silence" to "I'm not worth it," and the more balanced explanations feel like a dirt road that's hard to stay on. What strikes me is how you said that even when you *find* those other reasons, they just don't stick — which tells me this isn't about logic or effort, it's about the fact that that harsh belief has had so much more practice than the kinder one. What do you think that first thought — "they didn't want to deal with me" — is protecting you from feeling, if rejection weren't the answer?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, honestly. If rejection wasn't the answer... I guess I'd have to sit with not knowing why they went quiet, and that uncertainty feels almost worse than just deciding it's because I'm not worth their time. At least if I tell myself it's rejection, I feel like I have some kind of explanation, even if it hurts.
therapist: That's a really profound insight — your mind would rather have a painful answer than no answer at all, because uncertainty feels uncontrollable and the rejection story at least gives you something to hold onto. And the way you said that, quietly and carefully, makes me wonder if part of you already senses how exhausting it is to keep choosing that painful explanation just to feel some sense of control. What would it feel like to practice just sitting with "I don't know why they went quiet" — even for a moment — without rushing to fill that space with something harsh about yourself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, just hearing you describe it that way makes me feel kind of tired, like you've named something I've been carrying around without realizing how heavy it was. But I don't know if I can just sit with "I don't know" — that space feels almost worse than the rejection story, because at least the story is something I can mentally argue with or pick apart. The not-knowing just feels like floating in the dark with nothing to grab onto.
therapist: "Floating in the dark with nothing to grab onto" — that image is so vivid, and it tells me the uncertainty isn't just uncomfortable, it feels genuinely unsafe, like you need something solid to hold even if that something is painful. It makes complete sense that you'd reach for the rejection story, because at least it has edges you can feel and push against. I'm wondering if, over time, we might work on building you something else to grab onto in that dark space — not another harsh story, but maybe a different kind of anchor — and I'm curious what that might even look like to you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but honestly I don't even know what a different kind of anchor would look like. Every time I try to think of something positive or neutral to hold onto, it just feels... slippery, like it won't hold my weight the way the bad stuff does. I guess I'm skeptical that anything softer could actually feel real enough to matter when I'm really spiraling.
therapist: The way you describe positive things as "slippery" and unable to hold your weight is so telling — it's like the harsh beliefs have been load-bearing walls for so long that anything gentler feels like it couldn't possibly support you. And I notice there's something very quiet and careful in how you're saying all of this, like you're holding it gently rather than pushing it away, which makes me think part of you is genuinely open to the idea even while another part is protecting itself with skepticism. I wonder — rather than starting with something positive, what if the anchor we looked for was just something *true*, even if it's small and neutral, like a moment where someone's silence turned out to mean nothing at all?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client:
That's... actually an interesting way to put it. Not positive, just true. I think I can work with that more than trying to convince myself something feels good when it doesn't.

But I'm already trying to think of an example and my mind keeps going to times where the silence did mean something, where I was right to worry. It's like my brain has a much bigger filing cabinet for the evidence that confirms people are pulling away than for the times it turned out to be nothing.
therapist: What you just described has a name in CBT — it's called a confirmation bias, where our brain becomes a highly selective archivist, filing away everything that fits the story it already believes and quietly discarding the rest. And I noticed something shift a little when you said "I can work with that" — like something small but real opened up, even just for a moment. So let's start there: can you think of even one time, however small, where silence or distance turned out to mean nothing about your worth?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean... yeah, I guess there was this one time my friend didn't text me back for like three days, and I was convinced she was pulling away from me, that I'd said something wrong or just wasn't worth her time anymore. But then she called and it turned out she'd just been dealing with a family thing and hadn't been talking to anyone. I remember feeling relieved, but also kind of embarrassed that I'd spiraled so hard over it.
therapist: You just found one — and that's not nothing, that's actually a really important file to pull out of that cabinet. I want to gently push back on the embarrassment you felt about spiraling, because your brain was doing exactly what it's been trained to do, and it turned out the evidence just wasn't there this time. What do you think it would mean to let that memory count as real proof — the same weight as the times the worry turned out to be right?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech
